add a profile on the profiles tab: a link from the clipboard, a config file or a qr code. vless, vmess, trojan, shadowsocks, hysteria2, wireguard, tuic, naive and anytls are supported. pick it on home and hit START. the firewall, dns protection and TOR also run without any VPN profile.
tunnel — the whole device goes through the VPN.\nsplit — only selected apps, or everything except them.\nthe mode lives in apps → VPN routing. the authenticated LAN proxy is configured separately.

TOR passes traffic through three relays — sites see the exit relay ip, not yours. tcp only: udp, calls and streaming do not work. inside a VPN tunnel it is double protection — the isp sees only the VPN. the MODE button on home cycles VPN / VPN+TOR / TOR.

a smart profile bundles several protocols of one server — the smart label with a disclosure arrow in the list. ping under the protocol list runs the shared test: every enabled protocol is probed and its latency measured. the best one gets a mark and is used on connect.

the shared app lane follows the current VPN / TOR / VPN+TOR mode; block always denies network access. split can include or exclude the selected apps. site rules take domains and apply VPN, direct or block immediately through the active tunnel.

app — application and connection events.
net — the network journal: time, app, protocol, country, volume; it also feeds the map.
sec — the security journal: guard chain, app changes, anomalies.
journals are encrypted and never leave the device.

the map draws the tunnel path device → VPN → TOR; dashes are connections beyond the exit. the blue dot is the dns server currently answering queries. the map fills from the network journal; clearing its history leaves journals untouched.
local accounting of traffic, sessions and dns events: totals, profiles, apps, dns blocks, firewall and TOR. collection is opt-in and the data never leaves this device.

the local firewall blocks selected apps with no external server — even with the VPN off. anomaly analysis compares traffic against the usual baseline: upload spikes, background activity, new countries, dns block surges, frequent reconnects. events land in the sec journal.
the kill switch is a system android feature (“block connections without VPN”): if the tunnel drops, all traffic stops at the os level. enable it in the system VPN settings for FoxHole Guard.
settings → application → data: export profiles and settings to a file and restore them from one. the clear-data actions remove parts of the data; factory reset wipes everything and cannot be undone.

home is a terminal: every action echoes its canonical command — start VPN -p profile, start VPN+TOR, stop, restart, status, mode VPN / TOR / VPN+TOR, scan qr. commands stay in english; the answers follow the app language.\nstatus prints the active connections, exit ip · geo · isp and which apps go where. the log keeps the last 120 lines within the journal retention window.

while a route is up, dns goes through the tunnel and does not leak to the carrier dns server. dns bypass keeps chosen apps on the system dns server.\nthe guard also watches the system dns server set: if a network suddenly replaces every dns server, a security alert fires — the classic on-path substitution signal.

bind a profile to Wi-Fi or the mobile network. when the transport changes, the app recommends the bound profile — an in-app banner while the app is open, otherwise a notification with a one-tap switch.

share the connected tunnel with devices on the current wi-fi as a socks5/http proxy. authentication is mandatory — the proxy never starts with an empty password. the client↔phone hop adds no extra encryption: trusted networks only.

long-press a profile → edit: a structural editor for the protocol fields (server, port, transport, tls…). a smart profile keeps one entry per protocol. insecure tls always needs an explicit consent and is remembered per profile.

profiles arrive as a link from the clipboard, a config file or a qr code; subscriptions refresh from their url. long-press → select marks profiles for export to a file; share sends a single profile as a link or qr code.
settings → security: lock the app with a pin or biometrics; relock fires by timeout, instantly or on reboot. profiles, credentials and journals live encrypted on the device and never leave it.

Sentinel is local metadata analysis, not antivirus, and it does not read traffic payloads. App checks score installer source and declared high-risk capabilities; a signal is not proof of malware. The build ships a curated stalkerware list (612 package names and 471 signing-certificate digests, from AssoEchap/stalkerware-indicators, CC-BY-4.0); it covers stalkerware specifically, not malware in general. Traffic detection compares one-minute aggregate windows; per-app and background signals additionally require statistics and Usage Access. With a FoxHole PIN and event monitoring enabled, the guard records app installs, updates, removals, host heartbeats and suspected gaps in a sealed, hash-chained journal. Economy adds no permanent service; reinforced keeps a visible foreground service and can use more battery. Android force-stop pauses monitoring until FoxHole is opened again; root access and clearing app data cannot be prevented.
settings → application → updates: the geoip database (the map and geo facts) ships bundled; check for a fresh one manually or enable auto update.
home-screen widgets: status (connection state and quick commands) and web apps (icon grid with unread badges). each widget has its own background settings — black or white plus opacity.

with TOR active, choose a file, expiry and download limit. FoxHole copies it into a root-owned encrypted vault and publishes a session-only onion service; stopping TOR, expiry or revoke withdraws it and deletes the ciphertext. the invitation contains a 256-bit download capability as a basic-auth username, never in the url; an optional password is sent separately and is stored only as an Argon2 verifier. the recipient opens the invitation with TOR Browser. the sender side is download-only, capped at 512 MiB, and never falls back to LAN or clearnet. I2P publication is not available in this beta.

I2P is held up by its own users. Allow your device to pass other people\'s encrypted packets through and the network gets faster and harder to block for everyone.\n\nThis is safe: the traffic is encrypted end to end, your device cannot read it and is not its source or destination — it is one relay of many.
